utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, I should say to the Court that we are sorry to have kept you waiting. Matters took rather longer than anticipated, but we're ready now. We'll sit until 5.30. I hope it's possible to get through your cross-examination, Mr. Kovacic, as I said, expeditiously, so that we can make a start on the next witness. Do you anticipate managing to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm certain that I can be finished in maximum an hour, and probably a quarter more; not more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll take the break when you've finished and we've had the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Could I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Kovacic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Zeco.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Bozidar Kovacic. I'm an attorney from Rijeka, not from your Rijeka but another place called Rijeka, and I represent here Mr. Mario Cerkez. As you were told earlier on, if you do not understand my question, please tell me, and I will repeat it. Mr. Zeco, you have told us where you lived. You indicated the area on a photograph. A little lower down on the same road, the Cerkez family lived. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know the Cerkez family?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew very well the father and mother of Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Mario Cerkez also had a brother?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you knew both of them?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew the brother by sight, but I knew Mario Cerkez in person. However, I do not recall having any personal contacts with him. I only knew him by sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you knew the parents better. And could you tell us, on the basis of your knowledge of the family, what could you tell us about that family and the environment? Did you ever notice, among any member of that family, any sign of discrimination or prejudice based on religion or anything else, ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout my life in Vitez, and I lived there for 25 years, during that period, after the time when the unfortunate event occurred, I had absolutely no objections or criticisms to make of their behaviour. They were very friendly. Good neighbourly relations existed. I can only say words of praise about the family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear from anyone else anything that would be contrary to this opinion that you held?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, if somebody suddenly changes, would you consider that to be something normal?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question for me, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Never mind; let's leave that for the moment. Yesterday, talking about Rijeka, you said it was a neighbourhood community there which you knew extremely well, and you mentioned Darko Kraljevic as the leader of a unit called Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you knew Darko Kraljevic well, too, in view of the fact that you were neighbours?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that the Vitezovi were formerly HOS, and later on that they joined the HVO?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when the HOS joined the HVO?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was sometime in the second half of 1992, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Darko Kraljevic's unit, in this part of Vitez and further beyond, was very visibly present; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were a visible force that one had to reckon with, wouldn't you say?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Generally speaking, were people afraid of the members of that unit, the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least in the area of Rijeka itself, there were no visible reasons for fear, but there were stories and rumours about their activities. But I personally couldn't note anything of significance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were generally accepted rumours, according to what I have heard and we have heard here in court, that Darko Kraljevic had connections with drugs. Did you ever hear anything to that effect?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that this part of Vitez was virtually under the control of the Vitezovi, just before the outbreak of the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I think that this was part of an all-out Croatian movement, headed by the HVO, as a component of the civilian and military authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you would agree that the Vitezovi were a unit within the HVO?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you would also agree that they were a powerful unit?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the military sense, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that when they first came to your house and arrested you, that they came from the Sumarija building?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among them was this young man called Krunoslav Bonic?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that this young man, Krunoslav Bugojnoic, was only 16, that he was under age?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was very young. I didn't know exactly how old he was, but I knew him as a young boy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that he was of an age which would make him a military conscript?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had the appearance of a military man. He was dressed as a soldier and armed, and he gave the impression of a soldier, regardless of his age. He acted as a real soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, there were village guards in operation in the area?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us of any fact on the basis of which we could ascertain with greater certainty whether this particular young man, Krunoslav Bonic, was a member of the village guards or another grouping?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will repeat it, of course. Could you indicate any single fact that you knew of or heard of on the basis of which one could conclude which unit Bonic belonged to? Did he belong to village guards, the Vitezovi, the military police?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As in those days, and in those parts, I identified units belonging to the HVO movement as a whole without entering into their organisational structure, so that I thought them to be an army under the exclusive control and command of the HVO. I didn't concern myself with the actual structure and the units. I viewed them as a single unified army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for them, it was quite sufficient to know that they belonged to the HVO, and you as a citizen thought everything else to be irrelevant; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you even include village guards in that structure, even though they are not formally a part of the structure?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in touch with those guards. I was only thinking of people wearing military insignia, HVO insignia, and the most important -- the characteristic sign was the chequerboard emblem that they wore either on their sleeves or on their lapels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what about the uniform? Was that an indication of the unit a soldier belonged to?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were different uniforms. Some people wore uniforms that were not camouflage uniforms. There were those wearing black uniforms; they belonged to Darko Kraljevic's unit. Some of them also had black uniforms. But I was able to see the same people wearing, on one occasion, a black uniform and, on another, a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that if I understand you well, a uniform is not a reliable distinguishing sign.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but the most important thing was the chequerboard emblem, which was indicative of membership to a particular military grouping.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understand you well, the insignia are distinguishing signs, but the uniform in itself is not; is that so?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also told us about that unfortunate incident when you were caught up on the road, dragged out of the car, and physically assaulted. Is it true that this was done by the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was later told that they were Vitezovi. I was told by a representative of the police; whereas I personally, at that point in time, did not know which unit they belonged to. They were all wearing camouflage uniforms with HVO insignia, and later on, from police representatives, I learnt that they were members of the Vitezovi unit, which was under the command of Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Samija told you that, the person you mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having mentioned Samija, do you know anything about the circumstances under which he was killed?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told, at least in the course of our discussions at the level of the presidency, we were informed that Mirko Samija was killed by the HVO as being a disobedient subordinate, and that was the information we received officially in relation to Mirko Samija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of different interpretations or stories?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a rumour that on the road between Vitez and Busovaca, he was driving a car and that he was hit by a bullet; however, the date when Mirko Samija was killed was a time when there was no shooting by members of the army. So we accepted as fact that Mirko Samija had been killed by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to this version, he was killed near Buhine Kuce.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're talking about a summer when there were snipers and there were quite a number of casualties from sniper fire. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that there were any sniper nests then, at the time when Mirko Samija was killed, in that area. As far as I am aware, there were no snipers in that area at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can we agree that there were at least two versions of the killing of Mirko Samija?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you trust one version more than another?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, Mr. Kovacic, that we're going to be helped very much by this. It's based purely on rumour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I will move on. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the majority population in Buhine Kuce, Bosniak or Croat?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly about 50/50 Croats and Bosniaks in the wider area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that later on, as the war developed, late in 1993, there was very fierce fighting between the two parties?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that there were very high casualties on both sides there?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday that you knew that there were two components of the HVO government. Within that framework, talking about the police, you told us that Samija was the commander of the civilian police. Do you know who, in those days, was the commander of the military police in the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a person who was, in a way, involved in the organisation and activities of the authorities, do you know that between the military police and the civilian police there are clearly regulated differences regarding competencies?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't Samija actually tell you, when he told you what he knew, that simply he was not responsible, he didn't have the competence?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I have to say that I knew Mirko Samija as a highly qualified professional, because he was a municipal judge, and I had a great deal of trust in his professional approach. I had confidence in him and I expected him to act in accordance with all laws and regulations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that means that we can agree that the HVO, after Pero Skopljak left as the chief of police, Mirko Samija was appointed as the chief of police, even though he was a judge.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Mirko Samija was appointed to the position of head of MUP, there was an agreement between representatives of the Croats and the Bosniak representatives, and I know that at a meeting of the war presidency of Vitez municipality, we agreed and accepted the appointment of Mirko Samija as head of the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, and Saban Mahmutovic as the chief of police, which in those days was, in fact, carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So is it true that, generally speaking, among the population of Vitez, the fact that the HVO had, on the basis of an agreement reached at the crisis staff, appointed Samija as head of the police, was that something that was very well received by the citizenry?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mirko Samija was a prestigious person. As I have already said, he was a professional, a man of trust.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever learn later on who was in command of the military police or whom they belonged to, or any other details about the military police in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that this was not publicised, nor was any information released about that, so I have no insight into the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that you were arrested on the 16th of April by a group of soldiers, among whom was Bonic. They were the Vitezovi. They took you to the veterinarian station and they detained you there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned that the person responsible for detention was Zeljko Matkovic --

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- and that he belonged to the military police.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which military formation he belonged to. I just know that he was the leader and that he was in charge of the detainees held in the veterinarian station. I didn't know, in military terms, which unit he belonged to. I just knew that he was the commander of the camp where the detainees were held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you used the term "camp," what do you imply? According to what you told us yesterday, this can hardly be called a camp.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I told you that we were held in a gym, we lay on the floor, we were ordered around, we were locked up, we couldn't leave the place, we had no contact with others, except for what I've already told you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made a statement for the investigators of this Tribunal on the 14th of July, 1995, and let me just quote a sentence. You said, "Zeljko Matkovic, who was one of Kraljevic's men, asked me about plans later on that day when my car was seized." You told us yesterday that the car was taken away from you, but here in that statement you said Zeljko was Kraljevic's man, but today you say you don't know who he belonged to. How can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this smaller area of Sumarija, the veterinary station, Kraljevic's units were the most prominent, and that is what people believed. However, it is a fact that in the premises of Sumarija there was also the headquarters situated there, in the forestry administration; and among others, my colleague, a veterinarian who worked with me in the veterinary station, was a member of that command. He was in charge of the medical corps attached to the command of the Rijeka headquarters. So there were soldiers of the HVO and those specific units known as the Black Vitezovi of Darko Kraljevic, but all of them were there in the same limited area, the area of Sumarija, the veterinary station, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, but can you explain why in '95 you explicitly said that Matkovic was Kraljevic's man, and now you don't seem to know?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he was under the direct command of Darko Kraljevic but that he was a member of the HVO, of the HVO headquarters in Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is what you think?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think; that is what I claim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm asking you, on the basis of which facts?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because soldiers came from the headquarters, including this colleague of mine, the veterinarian, who was also involved in the headquarters. He would come, and they would exchange comments and converse with one another, whereas Darko Kraljevic's soldiers, only those came who asked Zeljko Matkovic for a certain number of soldiers, which he would place at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To who?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you mean HVO units?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would come to ask for a certain number of detainees to take for trench digging. And there were other soldiers, who did not belong to Darko Kraljevic's unit, who would also come to collect people to take them to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 30th of April I think you said that you were transferred from that place of detention in Sumarija to the school in Dubravica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in charge of that place, which you called a camp?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: HVO units were in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which HVO units?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I know that the commander of the camp was Plavcic, Marijan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, on the video clips that we were shown, we saw shots of the detention place in Dubravica, and there was a drawing on the wall with the words "Black Legion." Do you know that the Vitezovi were sometimes called "Black Vitezovi" or "Black Legion"?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that they were referred to in that way too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were many Vitezovi from your immediate neighbourhood. Did you see any one of them in Dubravica as being members of those forces?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't see anyone?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know exactly which HVO unit was in charge of Dubravica?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I just said that the members were members of the HVO, who were wearing the camouflage uniforms with the HVO insignia, and that the commander was -- at least he introduced himself as Marijan Plavcic, with whom I had a certain contact. We had requested for him to receive us. It was a delegation; I was a commander there. We wanted to discuss the issue of taking certain detainees to dig trenches, because without proper supervision, these prisoners were taken to dig, and it was about their physical conditions, that some of them were sleep-deprived. So we wanted them to work out lists, to produce lists and select people who were the best able to go to dig trenches, and this is what they did. So this list was then followed and complied with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I will move to that and ask you about it later, but I want to ask you about this person, Plavcic. Was this Marinko Plavcic, the son of Drago?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, oh, yes, it was Marinko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a deputy of Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him around Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zeco, is your intention to go back to Rijeka? That is what you said in your statement.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do the Vitezovi still have any kind of influence there? Do you know somebody who is with them?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat this for me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you afraid of Vitezovi today? Do you fear them still?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: By nature, I am not a very fearful person -- with respect to myself, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that when your car was taken away, you said that it was Vitezovi who did so; but yesterday, when you gave evidence, you didn't say that clearly. In the statement you made in 1995, you very clearly stated that in Sumarija, you were packed together -- this was in '93 -- soldiers of Kraljevic came and said that they wanted your car and that you gave them the car. So were they the ones who took the car, or the HVO, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did explain that a while ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So you don't know?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers who were dressed and who had come from Sumarija, I don't know whether they were Kraljevic's soldiers. I don't know. They were some HVO units. I didn't know them. They were all together. I know that they had come from Sumarija because my car was taken to the Sumarija's backyard. I know that they had taken it there. And as I said yesterday, I had disconnected the cables.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Those are details, and you've talked about that. But your answer needs to be either yes or no. When you spoke to the investigators in July of 1995, did you say that your car was taken by the Kraljevic men?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was possible? Thank you. When you said that different units were coming, both to Sumarija and to Dubravica school, looking for and taking prisoners out to dig trenches, you explained that these were the HVO soldiers, but you don't know which units. You agreed that there were Vitezovi among them. Do you agree that there were also units there which had come from outside of the Vitez municipality territory?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were soldiers, men there, whom I did not know; that is, the soldiers who had come to the camp and looked for people to go out and to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you cannot identify them by their insignia?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know the insignia, but the men I did not recognise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were released from the Dubravica school, you said that you were taken to the hotel and questioned there. Do you know whose headquarters this was where you were taken?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that. I only know that it was the military police. It was the military police which had come to take me, and they took me to the hotel. They were wearing white belts, and I assumed that they were the military police. So they took me to the hotel, where they brought me, as I said, into -- I know that it was a command there. I don't know which command, but there was a command post, some higher command in the hotel. General Blaskic was there in the hotel, but it was the first time that I entered the hotel when I was detained and brought there. And then yesterday I described how my arrest took place and how I was brought to the hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody among the military police with whom you communicated on that occasion introduce themselves to you, identify what unit they were from?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that this was a higher command. Did Mario Cerkez also keep his headquarters there?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, his headquarters was in the cinema, theatre building. His command was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was the workers' centre or the cinema theatre; that is what we're referring to?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was Cerkez there?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not see him there?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see him there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Cerkez was also not in Dubravica during the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in a position to leave the room in which I was detained throughout this time, until I was released, so that I could not see anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether you agree that the distance between the cinema theatre and the Dubravica school is somewhere between two and a half and three kilometres?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: About two and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little bit less, and about halfway there is the forestry administration building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is 1,5 kilometres from the cinema theatre to the Sumarija?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, somewhere around there. Maybe 1,2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let us just clear up one more thing. When your wife, along with Zvonko Santic, who had helped you, came back home to pick up some things, did soldiers again intervene?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say whether the soldiers who were there were Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know one of the soldiers by name. I was told this by my wife and Zvonko Santic. This man's name was Miro Kulic. He was one of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't know what unit he was with?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who he was with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, when asked, that you knew that in the civilian structure of the HVO, the top man was Ivica Santic?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was the brother of Zvonko Santic, who helped you?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were a member of the crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not come to the crisis staff sessions?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially, no, I did not, but on several occasions I was with representatives of the crisis staff. I came by a couple of times, perhaps twice. But this was not in an official function.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not come as a member, but I assume that if a certain issue was discussed --

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I did not interfere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall that as representatives of the military structures on both sides were on the one side Marijan Skopljak and on the other side Hakija Cengic? They were representatives of the military structures of the two organisations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Marijan Skopljak; that is not Pero Skopljak, whom you mentioned yesterday? That is somebody else?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that this Marijan Skopljak during 1992 was the chief of staff of the military structure of the Vitez HVO?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the meetings which you attended, this was during 1992?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Yesterday you said something about this approach of the HVO authorities in regard of the Muslims' employment, that they sort of started pushing them aside, that their positions were threatened, that they began being fired. You talked about your wife, but the fact is that your wife remained employed?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that is because she signed the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the other Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the war presidency, a decision was adopted that all employees should sign this document, that that was the official position of the leadership in the Vitez municipality, so that all employees -- I think that only two employees of the local government did not sign, and they had to leave their positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This means that instead of individuals deciding for themselves, the war presidency decided for them?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war presidency took a position that since the people had come asking what to do, since the legal authority should be suspended and that they were asked to accept the Herceg-Bosna government, so because of this, they asked the Bosniak representatives -- in this case, this was the war presidency, so they asked for a decision from us. Since this affected their very existence, they asked for a decision from us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So the war presidency adopted such a decision. Next, what I want to ask you, this document that is mentioned all the time, was there a particular wording? Was there a language there, "I swear allegiance," an oath or something? So what was it?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a preamble. It said: "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna," and then it was signed by the local government's president.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zeco, you were a state employee?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were laws. Were you receiving, perhaps once a year --

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever there was some kind of reorganisation, any changes of structure, we would receive certain decisions on assignments to certain jobs, positions, and we had salary scales and all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You needed to have some kind of a document. Very well. So in this particular case, they just received new documents, new decisions?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They received new decisions, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in the heading of these new decisions, there was "the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna," so to them, that meant pledging allegiance to this entity?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how this was interpreted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it never stated that in the decision itself.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that, as such, this decision, with all its details as you described them, was supposed to mean something, and people interpreted this as ignoring the legal authorities and a pledge of loyalty to the new organisation. Because at that time, the local parliament ceased to exist and people -- it was asked of people expressly to sign. If they didn't sign, they would be fired from their jobs. This was unusual; that had never been done previously, and so people asked assistance and some kind of intervention, which led to everything that I have then described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will agree that the municipal council had ceased to exist in its legal form and continued to exist as the crisis staff in 1992.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crisis staff only functioned in a sense that it had to deal with certain incidents and problems, and the crisis staff needed to come to certain solutions in order to overcome that crisis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was the crisis staff in which representatives of both ethnic groups were members?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zeco, you also said that you were in charge of civilian affairs in the presidency, and I assume that you knew the regulations which were in force in Bosnia and Herzegovina with respect to civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Since other people present today in the courtroom may not know all these regulations, could you describe what "work duty" meant in those regulations?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is something in connection with the civilian protection, there was also an obligation or duty for people to become involved in matters of civilian protection, if this is what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was one duty of citizens?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us some examples of what types of activities this involved?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were activities in the protection of civilians, of material goods, property, and other goods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's give an example. A bomb or a shell falls and a house is destroyed. Who would try to pull out the people from the rubble?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be the civilian protection; they would come to assist. We had wartime situations and we had cases where we had such interventions, especially around the Lasva River. There were units which were organised, and it was for different needs, should different needs arise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it involved the preparation of shelters, in case of attack, and the digging of trenches?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the tasks was the maintenance of such activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me just ask you one further question. Who were the people who were under this kind of obligation? Everybody?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was not clear. One additional question: Who, according to the law of that period, had the duty to perform such duties?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean who had these kinds of duties?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which citizens were duty-bound in civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the people who had work duty?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just give us an example. Let's say a citizen between 25 and 45, would such a citizen have primarily a work duty or some other type of duty?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some had work duty; some had combat duty, depending on their abilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So some citizens had work duty and some had military duty?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about women?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, women as well, yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the age limit for men for the work duty?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sixty years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So in the end, we did hurry up. You said a little bit about your moving to somebody else's house and somebody else moving into your house, but I think one issue remained unclear. Today in Bosnia, on the basis of various decisions of the High Commissioner of Bosnia, there are certain agencies and there are various administrations, cantonal and county, and there is an effort to bring everybody back to their home.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your case is now being processed. For instance, I know that in Ahmici, about 70 families came back.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about in the area of Rijeka? Did any families come back to Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps only a few individual cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, there are great differences from case to case.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there is an organised effort in the society as a whole to do this?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, there are a number of difficulties; I agree with that. The situation is very complex, and I can accept that as a fact, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zeco, I thank you very much for your answering all my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a few questions, a few clarifications that I would like to ask the witness to give us. Re-examined by Mr. Lopez-Terres:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zeco, during his cross-examination, Defence counsel for Mr. Kordic asked you whether, starting in January of 1993, there weren't two parallel governments that had been set up in Vitez, the first for the administration of the Croats and the second for the administration of the Muslims. Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I couldn't hear the interpreter very well, so could you please speak a little more loudly?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question. Mr. Kordic's Defence counsel yesterday asked you whether, starting in January of 1993, there was not in Vitez a parallel government set up, one for the administration of the Vitez Croats and the other for the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As regards the war presidency, which had been set up by the Muslims, wasn't it set up only to respond to the takeover of power of Vitez by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, in view of the fact that the legal existing authorities in the area of Vitez municipality had been suspended and that the Muslims did not participate in government, the Bosniaks organised themselves and formed a parallel government which was meant to perform regular duties, and what they did was form the war presidency of Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The suspension of the legitimate municipal authorities who had been democratically elected in 1990, was that suspension only because the HVO, who had taken power, had set up its own units in order to push the Muslims aside?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a question about Mr. Pero Skopljak, a person we spoke about today. Was he the police chief before Mirko Samija?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Skopljak, in April of 1993, was the president of the HDZ in Vitez? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Ivica Santic was the president of the HVO in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Darko Kraljevic was a person who was spoken about with you today. Did you know his family well?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a family that you liked?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As my neighbours, I had very close relationships with the Kraljevic family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever notice among Mr. Kraljevic's relatives that there was any kind of discriminatory behaviour towards the Vitez Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like us to go back now to the 16th of April, 1993, in the morning. The soldiers that came to your house, among whom was Krunoslav Bonic, whom you recognised, were they wearing black uniforms or camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was wearing a camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 2nd of May, 1993, when the soldiers came to your house in order to search it and then took you to Sofa, did you recognise Mr. Bonic again?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they wearing a black or a camouflage uniform; that is, the soldiers who were with him and Mr. Bonic?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the soldiers -- and I had noticed them already in the background. There were four or five of them -- they were all wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, 1993, when you were arrested by Bonic and the other soldiers who were with him, were those soldiers and Bonic members of the Vitezovi unit?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no information to tell me that they belonged to the Vitezovi. I don't think they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never said that Mr. Bonic was a Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As regards the veterinarian centre where you were detained, you said that the commander was Zeljko Matkovic.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he wear a black uniform or camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wore a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. A few moments ago, we spoke about the work obligation which citizens of the former Yugoslavia were obliged to do.

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those individuals who were detained with you, whether they were at the veterinary centre or at the Dubravica school, did they have to go to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could they, according to you, be considered as having been carrying out their work obligation?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, under no circumstances could they be considered to have been treated as performing their work duty, because the treatment they were given was simply inhumane; it was a treatment below any acceptable standard that would be applied to people performing work duty. These people were mistreated, provoked in all kinds of ways, and they were required to carry out certain assignments. So the people who went to perform such work, upon return, they came back physically and psychologically in very bad shape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these people have a choice of refusing to carry out that forced labour?

utterances.speaker: FUAD ZECO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those people had to go and they had to do as they were told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Zeco, for coming to the International Tribunal and giving your evidence. You are now released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now until 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat, Mr. Damon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm asking your permission just for one sentence to address the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we deal with this at the end of the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I just wanted you to reserve three minutes on the end for information I would like to provide in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Sayers has been kind enough to give me an indication of the paragraphs of the outline that we can move through quite quickly. Examined by Mr. Scott:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will start by cautioning both myself and Mr. Damon, because you and I speak the same language, we tend not to pause sometimes for the interpretation, so if both of us can be mindful of that, I'm sure the interpreters will appreciate it. Mr. Damon, I understand that you were actively involved as a journalist in southeast Europe from 1989 until the end of 1993, working as a freelance journalist, mostly for SkyNews; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: It's correct. I was there a little longer than that, until 1995, but in other respects it's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1989 you were initially based in Hungary, where you covered the breakdown of the former Yugoslavia and built a wide variety of contacts in the area, particularly in Belgrade and Zagreb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also correct to say that you covered the war in Slovenia and Croatia and were often quoted in a Croatian TV programme -- I will try: Slikom na Sliku?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. SkyNews was a satellite service and therefore was accessible to the broadcasters in the region, and they often recorded it and then put their own commentary over my pictures or would give a translation of my complete reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And following that time, is it accurate to say that you were in Bosnia itself, if you will, from approximately May 1992 to January of 1993, and then again from approximately April to December 1993, or perhaps thereafter?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout your time in Croatia and Bosnia from 1991 to 1994, is it correct that you had a good deal of success in travelling and getting through checkpoints, and also meeting politicians and military commanders, because your staff and interpreters were Hungarians from the Vojvodina, and they tended to be viewed, therefore, as independent?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: That's correct. We were operating as a small team, and so we had to be able to move across front lines, and so it was essential for us to appear to be objective and impartial. And the Hungarians, because they were not directly involved in the conflict, helped us to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it your experience that you seemed to be able to gain access and move more freely than some of the other journalists?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: I think so, because we genuinely did try to present an objective picture, and so we were allowed, after perhaps a great deal of persuasion, to go to places where others might not because they would be seen to be partial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, based on that, that you were able to interview a number of the more prominent people in the former Yugoslavia, including Radovan Karadzic on several occasions, and in fact you spent time with him in his villa in Pale; on another occasion, you interviewed the Bosnian Serb general Ratko Mladic at the Lukovica barracks. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were also able to meet and interview Bosnian president Izetbegovic and also the Bosnian Croat leader Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that in fact you met Mr. Boban approximately two or three times, at least once in Grude, once in Zagreb, and perhaps in other places on other occasions?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: Yes, I interviewed him directly on two occasions: once in the lobby of the Hotel Intercontinental in Zagreb and then again in Grude, at his offices. And then I met him at various meetings; not to interview, but to talk to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could depart from the outline just momentarily, perhaps it would be worthwhile to say: Who did you understand Mr. Boban to be at that time, and what was his role in these matters?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: He was the senior Croatian political leader in the part of Bosnia-Herzegovina claimed by the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct, sir, that on about the 24th or 25th of April, 1992, with the help of the Serbs, you actually flew into Pale by helicopter, and this was your first arrival in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: Yes, I met the so-called Serbian royal family, members of whom were trying to bring help to the Serbs in Bosnia. We were having some difficulty getting into Bosnia, and they offered to take us with them just on a visit to Pale, where they were flying to meet with Mr. Karadzic. And my wife, who was my camera operator at the time, and I decided that this was an opportunity that we should seize. So we went ostensibly just to go for the short visit, but we didn't come back, because we wanted to stay and cover the situation. We wore the same clothes for a number of days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct, Mr. Damon, that following that, in fact, you spent several weeks in Sarajevo, until approximately the end of May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: That's right, yes. Indeed, I think until early June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And is it accurate to say that there were approximately seven days in May, in fact, that you were the only western television journalist in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that to be correct. Most of the journalists were in the suburb of Ilidza, which was in Serb hands, came under attack by Bosnian Muslim forces, decided to evacuate very early one morning. And indeed, I went with them, because my wife -- who, as I say, was my camera operator -- was by that time very tired. So I went with her out to Split and then came back in, after a day, from Split to Sarajevo. My colleagues stayed in Pale, and I went down into the town, into the city of Sarajevo, and stayed in what later became the U.N. headquarters there. I by that time was doing my own filming, and took the pictures, and my colleagues came down during the day to collect the footage. And indeed it was transmitted from the TV station, a temporary TV station set up in Pale by the Serbs. They had a microwave link which went through to Belgrade and then into the Eurovision system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, following this experience in Sarajevo, after that, did you base yourself in a small village between Kiseljak and Busovaca, somewhere near the Catholic convent?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, in rooms above a cafe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you, from June to July in 1992, and thereafter, travel extensively in both central and western Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be accurate to say, Mr. Damon, that by the fall of 1992, you had spent a substantial amount of time in Kiseljak, Vitez, and Tomislavgrad, and travelled to the Dalmatian coast via the routes from Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf to Prozor and through to Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during your travels, you were arrested by the ABiH or Muslim army around Gornji Vakuf in around June of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: That's correct. This was on the occasion after I had been there in Sarajevo on my own. One of the other journalists there was a photographer, and we decided to go together to the coast, and we stopped in Gornji Vakuf for coffee and were arrested. We did look pretty strange by that time, after being without supplies and so on for some time. We were arrested by the Territorial Defence of the Bosnian Muslim army, and they took us to the HVO, to the Croatian army headquarters, and it was clear that that was the hierarchy, that the Territorial Defence, the Muslims, if you like, were at that point subordinate to the Croats [Realtime transcript read in error "Muslims"] in Gornji Vakuf. I can't speak for any other part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that you were, in fact, interrogated by an HVO officer?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were then released shortly thereafter, or how did you come to gain your freedom again?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: No, I think it was only that they were nervous of strangers. Once I was allowed to establish who I was, then they were very friendly. We had the right accreditation and so on. It was simply that here were two rather scruffy-looking strangers in the middle of their town, and they didn't know what we were doing there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, I don't know if this was just a transcription error or if you misspoke, but you said -- I think you repeated, you said, "... the Muslims, if you like, were at that point subordinate to the Muslims in Gornji Vakuf."

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: No, I said -- I meant to say "Croats," yes. It was the Croatian HVO which was at that time in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you tell the Court, during these various travels that you've described so far this afternoon around Bosnia, did you ever see the Croatian army, as distinct from the Bosnian Croat or HVO forces, did you ever see regular forces of the Croatian army in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: We, all of us, made the assumption that -- the logical assumption that the Croatian defence inside Bosnia was being supported and supplied by the Croatian army. There were occasions, particularly in the border town of Tomislavgrad, where we thought that we saw troops wearing Croatian army, as opposed to Croatian defence force, insignia. But there was one particular occasion which I do specifically remember because a truck with Croatian army plates came down a road where there were roadworks and, therefore -- we were going up the road -- we would have had to avoid the roadworks to move out onto the wrong side of road; and at this point, the truck came towards us, and so it was an incident which stuck in our minds. We commented then, those of us in the car, my translators and I, that this was Croatian army as opposed to HVO, and it was, I should say, a few kilometres inside the border of Bosnia. This was, to us, nothing exceptional because we made the assumption, which, I think, history and politics make very logical, that Croatia was supporting and the Croatian army was supporting its fellow nationals inside Bosnia. It was just the fact that it was a near-miss that made it something which sticks in my mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've used the word, in describing that, as "an assumption." Would it be fair to say that that was the conventional wisdom or thinking among you and the other journalists at the time?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: It was, and it makes sense because we know from the revelations of politicians, Western Politicians and others, how closely involved the Croatian government was, and, I suppose, in many ways, rightly so, in the period where the Bosnian army and the Croatian defence forces were in alliance against the Serbs, who were attacking. It seemed to us both sensible and necessary when there was very little support coming from the West.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any particular instance where you knew that there was some exchange among the senior officer ranks between the Croatian army or the HV and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: Yes. I was reading not very long ago a piece of paper that was photocopied and handed to me back in that year, 1993, a statement made by the new commander of the Croatian defence forces in Bosnia, Ante Roso, asking for the soldiers of the HVO to honour the dead of Croatia in previous wars by not committing atrocities on the battlefield. There had, of course, been by that time -- we're talking late 1993 -- there had been a great deal of evidence of atrocities, and I believe he was trying to regain the morale of the Croatian defence forces in Bosnia by saying that, and we knew that he had previously been a senior commander in the Croatian army. Again, I'd like to stress, I can't see anything wrong with that if the battle is for the protection of those who are under attack in alliance, but, of course, the situation of the alliance became untenable for a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you should make your statement a bit more clear. What are you addressing now?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: Well, there is -- there's no doubt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you just for a moment. This is Mr. Damon's opinion about a particular matter. We are, of course, concerned with the facts. Where his opinion is relevant to the case, with respect to him, we'll hear it, but I don't think this, at the moment, is helping us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I fully agree, Your Honour, obviously, if it is, in fact, based upon opinion or assumption. I'm not sure that's where Mr. Damon is going with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, I'll caution you. If you are only talking about opinion or speculation, we can move on. If you have some other basis to further address the question, then I'd ask the Court to allow you to.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: No. I was only suggesting -- I was trying to reinforce the logic of what had happened, that's all, that it happened and it was logical that it happened, that a senior commander from the Croatian army should come to lead the Croatian defence forces in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let us move on. So the record is clear, is it fair to say or correct that you did not, in your travels, to your recollection, see any HV troops yourself in the area; for instance, around Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: That's correct. I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that your first direct contact with the HVO was with Vinko Lukic, who was a police chief in Kiseljak, in the fall of 1992, and this apparently was in the circumstance of you and your crew wanting permission to work around or cover a larger area, and Mr. Lukic informed you that you had to get or needed to get permission from Colonel Blaskic at the time in order to move around in that fashion? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: That's correct. Indeed, on one occasion, we went to Mr. Lukic's house in order to try to achieve that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was, in fact, Mr. Lukic who ultimately did get you in touch with Colonel Blaskic on the first occasion.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: That is so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court -- I'm directing your attention to approximately the 26th of October, 1992. Did you and/or one of your video crews film what appeared to be an HVO training camp?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. I wasn't there, but the crew was sent off. I was doing another story, and they filmed training, which we used subsequently in an edited report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally see and edit that tape?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall or tell the Court what was the condition or quality of these troops that were caught on tape on the 26th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: This was a very efficient and well-trained squad. They were going through mock parachuting and so on, and other training, and it was clear that they were very good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that they did not appear at all to be anything like what might be described as a "rag-tag army"?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: Not at all. These were not villagers thrown together in a militia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could direct the video booth to the videotape excerpt which has been marked -- I understand the booth is referring to the last four digits of the video reference itself, as opposed to the exhibit number. I should say, for the record purposes, it's been marked as Prosecution Exhibit 257.1, but I think for the video booth it is 1086. I'd like to play that at this time, if we could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court if you can observe during this, Mr. Damon, what we can call now the traditional chequerboard insignia on the berets.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that, but I believe this is the shield of the HVO, not the HV.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps at this juncture, the video booth can just leave it -- if we can play it in fast-forward so that we can quickly get a feel for the tape without taking too much of the Court's time. Do you know what kind of weapons those were, that were just being held?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: I think they're pump-action shotguns. I'm not sure. I'm not a military expert.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all right. I think the record would be correct, and I don't think there would be any good-faith dispute, that from someone who knows more about weapons than probably most of us in the courtroom, this is a grenade launcher?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's it. Mr. Damon, did it come to your attention sometime during your stay in Bosnia, and directing your attention in particular to perhaps the latter part of 1992 and taking us into 1993, did you ever learn that the HVO had adopted some policy or decision not to let Muslims -- the Muslims in Bosnia participate in military training, or at least not military training being conducted by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: Yes. I heard this -- well, there were two different instances. I heard in Tuzla from a member of the Bosnian army that the Muslims had been ordered to hand in their weapons. The occasion you refer to of not being able to take part in training, I think that was -- again we heard that on several occasions. In Travnik, for example, I remember having a conversation with some soldiers of the Bosnian army there, but I can't remember the dates. By October 1992, it was very clear that relations between the two former allies had gone very badly wrong. There was an occasion when we were unable to travel one night when we were going back -- I was going back to meet my wife, who had stayed in Zenica, and I was with another camera operator, and we had to overnight in Bugojno; and then the following day, we drove through -- more or less through the middle of -- fairly low level, but a battle between the Bosnian army and the Croatian defence forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me direct you to, and direct the video booth to, please, a video marked as Exhibit 759.1, which is referenced as 1064, and if you could cue that up, please. I'll ask you, Mr. Damon, when you see the beginning of this piece, do you recognise this as a video that you or your crew took. So I guess we can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your voice, Mr. Damon?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, just looking at my notes, and we can do this another way if it's necessary, but would you date that tape approximately sometime between the end of April 1993 and the beginning of May 1993?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: Well, the dates are on the boxes from which the tape was taken. I really don't remember, but as we filmed them, we dated them. I believe there's no dispute about the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on. Did you, in fact, meet Colonel Tihomir Blaskic on several occasions while in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it your understanding that Mr. Blaskic's -- excuse me, Colonel Blaskic's command area extended from approximately the Kiseljak area up north and northwest to Travnik?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: That's what I was led to believe, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you form an opinion, sir, that Blaskic was a disciplined and professional soldier, that his troops appeared to like him, at least in general, and he was commanding an organised and well-disciplined military region?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: Yes, I found him to be a very proper officer. You could talk to him and negotiate, for example, passes to cross checkpoints and so on, and he behaved very correctly with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it appear to you that the HVO forces themselves were an organised, disciplined army?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: In large measure. Of course, there were plenty of people operating in what would not be considered to be a proper and orderly manner, but, yes, he had -- Colonel Blaskic had control. He was very much looked up to and deferred to by the troops operating in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, then -- we may have touched on this earlier -- your first personal contact with Colonel Blaskic was to get a pass in order to pass through HVO checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: That's the case, yes. I can't --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: I was only going to say I can't remember which checkpoints, but I remember that was the purpose. Indeed, I've still got the pass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that you, on this occasion, met Colonel Blaskic at his headquarters at the Hotel Vitez, after first speaking to several lower ranking persons before you were allowed to see Colonel Blaskic, and that you recall -- is it correct that you recall someone coming in from a side room and Colonel Blaskic telling them to type out a pass, that you then witnessed Colonel Blaskic sign the pass, and it occurred to you that this was something that was important enough to Colonel Blaskic that he would not let his subordinates deal with it themselves?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: Yes, all of that's correct. He signed it there and then for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, again, so the record is clear, is it fair to say, sir, that you do not recall ever meeting a man named Mario Cerkez or having any direct dealings with him yourself?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: I don't recall that; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever heard of Mr. Cerkez? I'm not asking you to express an opinion, but I'm just saying, did you in fact -- do you recall, during your travels and coverage in Bosnia, hearing the name "Mario Cerkez"?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: Yes, I heard him discussed, but I can't say when. And of course, since then I've had conversations about him, so it would be unfair to say when at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall generally whether what you knew and heard of him, in your professional journalistic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's be careful about this. The witness has been careful to distinguish between or to say that there are some things which he learnt at the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- and others which he's heard later. Is it realistically possible to distinguish between those, Mr. Damon?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: I wouldn't want to make that distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Damon, is it correct that you then -- you went to the village of Ahmici for the first time sometime on about the 24th or the 26th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: That's correct. I believe it to be the 24th, when U.N. ambassadors were visiting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court whether, by that particular date, had the atrocities or the believed atrocities in Ahmici become more widely known to the international community and, in fact, the media?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: Yes, my colleagues from BBC and ITN had transmitted footage which had alerted us all to what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you very briefly relate to the Court what you saw at Ahmici when you first went there on approximately the 24th of April?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON
utterances.text: What I first saw was the mosque, which was blown up and the minaret collapsed into the roof, and then one noticed, as one walked up the lane, the dead animals. And then we came to various houses which were burned out, and in the porch of one of those houses, there was a body; I don't know what age or -- it wasn't a child, but an adult body -- almost completely carbonised, and with what was most horrifying -- I don't know if any of us were capable of horror by then, but what was most horrifying was the hand, which was frozen in a kind of attitude of grasping, carbonised.
